lead: Malaria in pregnancy is mostly P. falciparum. Reduced immunity and parasites that bind the placenta make it more severe: it causes anaemia, hypoglycaemia, pulmonary oedema, miscarriage, low birth weight and stillbirth.
f: Uncomplicated: symptoms + parasites, no severe feature, can take oral drugs · Severe: parasites + any severe feature · Placental (silent): parasites without fever; harms the fetus; the target of IPTp · Severe features: impaired consciousness, repeated fits, Hb below 7, glucose below 40 mg/dL, temperature over 40 °C, parasitaemia over 5%, jaundice, blackwater urine, pulmonary oedema, renal failure, shock

sc: No fever, anaemia, small baby → Placental malaria

f: Primigravidae (no immunity to placenta-binding parasites), young mothers, non-immune women, HIV, no net or IPTp · Sticky infected red cells block small vessels and bind placental CSA · Pregnancy adds hypoglycaemia (parasites use glucose; quinine releases insulin) and pulmonary oedema

tr: Check blood glucose in every case; do not flood her with fluids

f: Fever, rigors, sweats, headache, vomiting; can mimic labour pains · Pallor, splenomegaly, mild jaundice · Many have no fever: anaemia or a small baby may be the only clue · Fever in pregnancy in an endemic area: test for malaria first · Thick film (parasites, density), thin film (species, % parasitaemia), RDT · Negative but suspicious: repeat the film · Severity: glucose, FBC, creatinine, bilirubin, urine output, fetal heart, growth scan

sc: Febrile, RDT negative, still suspected → Repeat the blood film

f: Fever: pyelonephritis, typhoid, chorioamnionitis, brucellosis · Fits or coma: eclampsia, meningitis, hypoglycaemia, epilepsy · Jaundice: hepatitis (E is severe in pregnancy), HELLP, AFLP

sc: Fit, fever, BP 110/70, film positive → Cerebral malaria
Fit at 34 wk, fever 39 °C and BP 160/110 → Treat both: MgSO₄ + IV artesunate

f: Maternal: anaemia (commonest), hypoglycaemia, cerebral malaria, renal failure, pulmonary oedema, shock, preterm labour, PPH · Fetal: miscarriage, preterm birth, stillbirth, FGR and low birth weight, congenital malaria

Decide by severity, not trimester · Uncomplicated: artemether–lumefantrine 4 tablets twice daily for 3 days in every trimester, with fatty food or milk; repeat a dose vomited within 30 min · Second line in the second and third trimester: DHA–piperaquine; no ACT: oral quinine 7 days · Severe: IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 h, then daily (IM if no vein) · Second line IV quinine 10 mg/kg 8-hourly in dextrose, with glucose checks · After at least 24 h IV and able to swallow: full 3-day oral ACT

sc: Fever again on day 3 of AL → Repeat the film; treatment failure → change drug
Confused and sweating on IV quinine → Check blood glucose (quinine releases insulin)

f: HDU, left lateral, airway, O₂ · Glucose at once, film, Hb, creatinine; IV artesunate now · Fits: diazepam, or MgSO₄ if eclampsia is possible · Careful fluids, catheter, hourly urine · Hypoglycaemia: 50 mL 50% dextrose then 10% infusion · Severe anaemia: Hb below 5 (below 7 after 36 wk): slow packed cells · Pulmonary oedema: sit up, O₂, stop fluids, furosemide · Shock: fluids, cultures, ceftriaxone · Labour: CTG, CS for obstetric reasons only; film on the newborn

IPTp-SP (3 tablets, observed) from 13 wk at every scheduled visit at least 4 wk apart, at least 3 doses (WHO); local clinics often give two · Insecticide-treated net every night, indoor spraying, iron and folate

tr: No SP in the first trimester or with cotrimoxazole; folic acid 0.4 mg, not 5 mg
No primaquine in pregnancy (fetal G6PD haemolysis)
